raw_response:
I'm 70 years old now, and I've been farming these 13 mu for 50 years. My old lady is 68, and it's just the two of us living here. Our son works in a factory in Shijiazhuang and only comes back for Spring Festival. We can't do the heavy work anymore — my back aches after half a day, and her knees swell up. So we have to hire people for harvest and the busy times. That costs money, but what can we do? The land doesn't wait.

For wheat, I always plant around October 8th, give or take a few days depending on when the autumn rain comes. I buy the improved seed from the county supply store — it's about 25 yuan per mu. I used to save my own seed, but three years ago I did that and the yield was poor, the kernels were small. Now I buy fresh every year. It's money out of my pocket, but it's worth it. Before planting, I put down one full bag of compound fertilizer per mu — that's 50 kg. I spread it with a bucket and then the rotary tiller works it in. In late March, when the wheat starts turning green, I look at the color. If it's a bit yellow, I topdress with half a bag of urea per mu. Last year fertilizer was expensive and I thought I'd save money by skipping the topdress — I lost maybe 50 kg per mu, and I regretted it all summer. So this year I'll do the topdress even if it hurts my wallet. Better to waste a little money than to lose the crop.

I irrigate wheat four times: once before winter to help it survive the cold, once when it turns green in March, once at jointing around Qingming, and once when the grain is filling in late May. The electricity for the pump costs about 20 to 25 yuan per mu each time, but wheat is our main grain and cash crop, so I don't skip irrigation. The well water is getting lower though — I've noticed it takes longer to pump each year. That worries me.

For maize, the window is tight. As soon as the wheat comes off in early June, I need to get the maize in within two or three days before the soil dries hard. I hire a tractor with a rotary tiller and a planter because I can't walk 13 mu behind a hand planter anymore. The hybrid seed costs about 45 yuan per mu. I put all the fertilizer in at planting — one bag of compound fertilizer per mu, and I add a scoop of urea in the seed furrow too, maybe 15 kg per mu. There's no time for split application; the season is short and I need to get it covered fast. I irrigate maize twice — once right after planting if the weather is dry, and once at the big flare stage in August. Usually the summer rains help, so two times is enough. If it rains too much, I worry about waterlogging, but that's better than drought.

For pests, I spray herbicide on wheat once in early spring — the wild oats are bad on my land. For maize, I spray herbicide after planting and insecticide once in August if I see armyworms. Two years ago the bugs were terrible and I had to spray twice. This year I'll watch and see.

Labor is our biggest headache. Between the two of us, we can handle the day-to-day things — turning on the pump, spreading fertilizer by hand, watching the fields. But for wheat harvest, maize planting, and maize harvest, we hire workers. The custom combine for wheat is 60 yuan per mu, and then we need young men to help load the grain onto the cart — that's 2 or 3 days of hired labor. For maize planting and harvest, we hire another 4 or 5 days. Workers want 150 yuan a day now, plus cigarettes and lunch. It's expensive, but without them the crop would rot in the field.

I expect about 450 kg per mu for wheat and 480 kg per mu for maize. Last year we got about 430 kg wheat and 460 kg maize because the spring was dry. The soil is good flat land, but we're getting old and can't manage it as well as we used to. My neighbor Old Wang, who's 65, gets 500 kg wheat, but he has his two sons helping him. I don't have that luxury.

This year I'll spend about 9,800 yuan on seeds, fertilizer, pesticide, electricity for pumping, and hired labor. That eats up most of our savings. I keep a little cash aside for medicine — at our age, you never know. I'd rather tighten our belts and eat simple than skip fertilizer and risk a bad year. A bad harvest hurts more than a good harvest helps, that's what 50 years has taught me.
